gm.name: Romania
gm.road_lines: White Outside - White Inside / Yellow Outside - Yellow Inside

items.html: Romania uses standard long, white European plates with a single blue strip on the left.

Romanian is a Romance language similar to Italian, containing the following special letters:

  • Ă ă
  • Ș ș
  • Ț ț

These letters are also found in some other European languages:

  • Â â, used in French, Portuguese and Turkish
  • Î î, used in French, Turkish and Italian

Additionally, in Turkish you can find the letter Ş, which can be confused with the Romanian Ș.

The most common types of utility poles in Romania are holey poles with the holes going all the way to the bottom. The holes are typically either quite wide or quite tall.

NOTE: Poland and Hungary also both use holey poles. Polish holey poles do not have holes near the bottom and Hungarian holey poles generally have smaller holes than in Romania.

Round concrete poles are also quite common.

NOTE: These are very similar to poles found in Bulgaria.

Trees and poles will often have white painted bottoms.

NOTE: This is also common in Ukraine and parts of Russia.

This type of extremely large yellow pole sticker is specific to Romania.

Beware that smaller stickers are also common and that both Bulgaria and Hungary can have similar ones.

NOTE: The town or city name will typically be written close to the middle of these stickers. In this case Podu Iloaiei is written.

Two support bars holding up the metal bar on pole tops, resembling an upside down triangle, can sometimes be found in Romania.

NOTE: Czechia, Slovakia, Albania and Serbia also feature this pole top.

It is very common to see waystones in Romania. They are typically fairly large, with red or blue framing with the road number on the side, or made of actual stone and somewhat rugged-looking. There is also a very small variant which is all white.
While there are many types of roadlines in Romania, these outer lines, consisting of short dashes with narrow spaces, can be a good clue for the country.
Middle lines are often noticeably thicker than average. This is especially useful to tell Romania apart from Bulgaria, which generally has thinner road lines.
Romanian directional signs are blue, arrow shaped, and have a white border. They will very often display the road number, which can be either red or blue.

The most common type of town entry sign in Romania is a yellow sign displaying a speed limit and a city skyline, with a white sign displaying the town name below.

NOTE: The upper sign can also either be white or completely absent.

Romanian sign backs are often black.

NOTE: This is also common in Italy, Albania and Germany.

Romanian chevrons are red on white, often with a yellow frame.

NOTE: Several eastern and central European countries have the red on white chevrons, however yellow frames are by far the most common in Romania.

Romanian bollards are thin and white, with a red vertical strip near the top. It is worth noting that bollards in Romania are somewhat rare.

NOTE: Turkey has a very similar bollard.
This yield sign, with an extremely thick red border, with a thin white outline, is unique to Romania. Beware that different yield signs also exist in Romania.

Romanian architecture primarily consists of single-family houses made of stone, typically painted in different pastel colours and with roofs ranging from orange tiles to grey metal. It is also somewhat common to see houses with walls made of painted square tiles in different patterns.
The Romanian landscape ranges from tall forested mountains and hills in the centre to flat or rolling agricultural landscapes in the south, west and east.
This type of haystack, typically featuring a stick going straight through, is very common in Romania.

Dacia is the most common car brand in Romania, making up more than a quarter of all vehicles in the country.

NOTE: No other eastern European country has more than 10% Dacias.
This is an elevation map of Romania. The tallest mountains are found in the middle and north of the country, while the south and west are particularly flat.

Completely flat agricultural landscapes can be found in the south and west.

NOTE: If you can see distant hills or mountains to the north, you are likely in the south, and if you see them to the south or east, you are likely in the west.
If you see several houses and almost all of them have orange tiled roofs, you are likely to be in the western half of the country.
Similarly, if you see several houses and almost all of them have metal or plastic fake tiled roofs, you will probably be in the eastern half of the country.

Villages near the Hungarian border will often be built in the same style as villages in Hungary. This style can be summarised as having long, straight streets with single-storey houses being evenly spaced along the road, typically having the short side of the house facing the road. The vast majority of roofs will have orange tiles.

South of Iași, near the border to Moldova, you can find rolling agricultural valleys with a very specific north-north-west to south-south-east angle.

NOTE: Make sure to look for agricultural fields on top of the hills to confirm this region.
Bilingual signs with Hungarian are mostly found in the central regions of Covasna, Harghita and Mureş, but also less commonly near the Hungarian border.
Elaborately decorated wooden gates are commonly found in the region of Maramureș.
Sunflowers are primarily found in the far east of the country, and secondly in the far west.
Several Romanian cities and towns have unique street signs. This infographic covers all with a population above 100 000.
The 67C is a mountain road with all yellow road lines.
The 7C is recognisable as going through some of the most dramatic mountains in Romania. The highest point on the road is right by the border between Sibiu and Argeș.
This type of window, shaped like a squinting eye, is most commonly found in the city of Sibiu.
If you see a mountainous landscape in Generation 2, you are likely close to Brașov.
Flat landscapes in Generation 2 are mostly found near Bucharest.

A boat trekker, with a green boat, can be found in the far east of the country. It mostly goes through small, overgrown canals in a flat landscape.

NOTE: There is no road coverage in this region.

lm.name: Romanian General Tips
lm.note:
Romanian is a romance language and thus more similar to Italian/French/Spanish then to the languages of it's neighboring countries. It also uses many unique characters and patterns that make it easy to recognize with a little bit of practice.

  • ă ș ț, unique characters

  • Â â, used in French, Portuguese and Turkish

  • Î î, used in French, Turkish and Italian

  • Common words: și, de, la, a, ai, ale, alor, cu

  • Word endings: -a, -ă, -u, -ul, -ului, -ție (or -țiune), -ment, -tate;

  • names ending in -escu

  • Double and triple i: copii, copiii

Note that Romanian is sometimes written online with no diacritics, making it harder to identify. A cedilla is sometimes used on S (ş) and on T (ţ) instead of the correct diacritic, the comma (above).

lm.name: Romanian Helpful Words
lm.note:
Here are a few words in Romanian that can either help you identify the language quickly, be helpful in region guessing, or just help learn the general feel of the language:

  • piese (auto) - car parts
  • cu excepţia - except (with exception)
  • preţ - price
  • de vânzare - for sale
  • magazinul - SHOP
  • preturi mici - low prices
  • Bucuresti - Bucharest
  • amenda - fine
  • interzisă - prohibited
  • plajă - beach
  • stradă - street
  • bulevard - avenue
  • atenţie - attention
  • biserică - church

lm.name: Street in Romanian
lm.note:
Stradă is the word for street in romanian. It's often shortened to "str." Careful! It can often be seen without the breve which makes it the same word as the italian "strada", however, most streets in Italy use the word "via".

Here are some other words similar to street in romanian: bulevard/bulevardul - avenue/boulevard piaţă - square/market calea - way intrarea - entry/entrance aleea - alley

lm.name: East - Metal & Fake Tiled Roofs
lm.note: • If you see several houses and almost all of them have metal or plastic fake tiled roofs, you will probably be in the eastern half of the country.

lm.name: West - Orange Tiled Roofs
lm.note: • If you see several houses and almost all of them have orange tiled roofs, you are likely to be in the western half of the country.

lm.name: Chevrons
lm.note:
• Romanian chevrons are red on white, often with a yellow frame.

--- NOTE:

  • Several eastern and central European countries have the red on white chevrons, however yellow frames are by far the most common in Romania.

lm.name: Hungarian Border - Hungarian Style
lm.note:
• Villages near the Hungarian border will often be built in the same style as villages in Hungary.
  • This style can be summarised as having long, straight streets with single-storey houses being evenly spaced along the road, typically having the short side of the house facing the road.
  • The vast majority of roofs will have orange tiles.

lm.name: Maramureș - Decorated Wooden Gates
lm.note: • Elaborately decorated wooden gates are commonly found in the region of Maramureș.

lm.name: Single Family Houses
lm.note:
• Romanian architecture primarily consists of single-family houses made of stone, typically painted in different pastel colours and with roofs ranging from orange tiles to grey metal.
  • It is also somewhat common to see houses with walls made of painted square tiles in different patterns.

lm.map: A Learnable Meta World - Poles - Beginner
lm.name: Holey pole
lm.note: Concrete holey poles with wide holes and usually painted white at the bottom are common in Romania. They are similar to poles in Poland and Hungary, but Polish poles have smaller holes that don’t go all the way to the bottom or top, and Hungarian poles typically have smaller holes as well.

lm.name: Architecture - 3D Tiles
lm.note: Houses made of decorative, colourful, 3D tiles are sometimes found in the northwest and Caraș-Severin county.

lm.name: Architecture - Arches
lm.note: Towns and villages in the southern plains are often identifiable by how often you’ll find houses with arches, either supplementing walls or as an extension over a veranda or entrance. There is also a separate cluster in the hills of western Bacău county.

lm.name: Architecture - Banat Houses
lm.note: In Banat and to a lesser extent the rest of the flat west, you can find a distinct architecture consisting of relatively plain houses, perpendicular to the street, with two small rectangular windows on the gable. More complex Dutch-like gables and brick-lined edges are even more unique to this area.

lm.name: Architecture - Baroque Houses
lm.note: Less commonly in the Banat region you can find similar houses with interesting and unique baroque-style roof shapes.

lm.name: Architecture - Beige Stones
lm.note: In northern Cluj county you can sometimes find these thin, messy beige stones used as a construction material for walls and houses.

lm.name: Architecture - Bistrița Houses
lm.note: Bistrița houses often have the narrower side facing the street, with the distinctive feature being the roof flap across the gable, a feature not found in western houses.

lm.name: Architecture - Black Tiles
lm.note: In Suceava county you can often find black plastic roof tiles, mimicking the general trend of northern mountainous counties having darker roofs in general. These are not unique to Suceava, but are far more common there, so it is generally recommended to use this meta if you see more than one house with such a roof.

lm.name: Architecture - Brick Edges
lm.note: Also in the western plains of Romania you will commonly find buildings with these small bricks lining the ends of roofs. These are also found commonly in Caraș-Severin county.

lm.name: Architecture - Bucovina Patterns
lm.note: Bucovina is a historical region that roughly corresponds to Suceava county. This specific style of decoration along the borders of walls and windows is a feature of Bucovina architecture.

lm.name: Architecture - Caraş-Severin Houses
lm.note: In Caraş-Severin, you will very commonly find houses connected and lined parallel to the street, giving a more closed feel. This is a very good way of identifying the county, especially in combination with wooded hills surroundings.

lm.name: Architecture - Cluj Jesus
lm.note: In Cluj county you will very often find this specific style of cross planted in people’s front gardens or by the roadside. It is distinctive for its decorated semi-circular arch above the statuette.

lm.name: Architecture - Concrete Bollards
lm.note: Specifically in the southern part of Székely Land, in Covasna county, these concrete bollards with a ball on top are common at property entrances.

lm.name: Architecture - Constanța & Tulcea Stone Walls
lm.note: In the far southeast it is common to find stone walls or wall bases in villages, often painted white.

lm.name: Architecture - Corrugated Roofs
lm.note: Dark coloured, corrugated metal roofs are extremely common in Maramureș. Note they are not unique to the county, but Maramureș is the only area where they are dominant.

lm.name: Architecture - Crocodile Tiling
lm.note: These crocodile-scale wall tiles are common in northern, mountainous parts of the country, particularly in Maramureș and Suceava.

lm.name: Architecture - Danube Delta
lm.note: Tulcea county, especially around the Danube delta, has very distinct Lipovan-Russian architecture. The key elements are thatched roofs, sky-blue elements anywhere on the house, and carved wooden gables with finials.

lm.name: Architecture - Decorated Gables
lm.note: Intricate wooden carvings can be found as gable ornaments in a band stretching from Cluj county to the mountains bordering Neamț county.

lm.name: Architecture - East Carpathian Barns
lm.note: In parts of the Eastern Carpathians you can find these barns with a wooden top part that is wider than the bottom, with vertical planks, often with thin openings.

lm.name: Architecture - Fence Benches
lm.note: Small covered benches integrated in fences, usually next to a gate, are common in an area covering Cluj and Sălaj counties.

lm.name: Architecture - Fence Tops
lm.note: Fences with a wide metal cover on top are super common in the northeast and Maramureș. Note that while they can be found occasionally outside these areas, streets completely lined with these fences will usually be in the northeast, particularly nearer the mountains in Neamț and Bacău counties.

lm.name: Architecture - Flaky Tiles
lm.note: These small, often flaky-looking black roof tiles can be found in the southern and eastern foothills of the Carpathians.

lm.name: Architecture - Fortified Churches
lm.note: Fortified churches are a feature of numerous towns and villages in formerly Transylvania Saxon populated parts of Central Romania, as well as Székely land.

lm.name: Architecture - Hat Roofs
lm.note: In Neamț county you can sometimes find these ‘elongated onion’ variants of hat roofs above the entrance of houses.

lm.name: Architecture - Indented Roofs
lm.note: Indented, mansard-like roofs are found throughout northwestern Romania. In certain regions like the Apuseni foothills, they are the dominant roof type.

lm.name: Architecture - Maramureș Barns
lm.note: In the southwestern part of Maramureș county (south of Baia Mare) you will find barns with particularly ornately-carved wooden walls and gables.

lm.name: Architecture - Maramureş Churches
lm.note:
Maramureş has a lot of wooden churches, with black-tiled roofs and particularly tall spires. The unusually tall spires can also be found on non-wooden churches in the region.

Wooden churches can also be found in the Apuseni mountains, however these are usually more modest.

lm.name: Architecture - Maramureș Gable
lm.note: These specific wooden gable features, often consisting of downward-pointing pikes in a row forming a small triangle at the top of the gable, are a feature of Maramureș architecture, particularly in the eastern half of the county.

lm.name: Architecture - Maramureș Gates
lm.note: In Maramureș you can find many intricately carved wooden gates at the entrance of properties.

lm.name: Architecture - Maramureș Wells
lm.note: In Maramureş county, it is common to find small circular/octagonal wells with conical roofs on people’s properties.

lm.name: Architecture - Maramureș Wood Houses
lm.note: Houses made entirely of wood, especially dark-coloured wood, can be found in most mountainous areas but are by far most common in eastern Maramureș county.

lm.name: Architecture - Metal Ornamentation
lm.note: In the east, especially the northeast, it is very common to find metal ornamentation of various types on roofs and under gables. Metal roofs in general are also more common in these regions, but are common enough in the south to be unreliable as a meta.

lm.name: Architecture - Modern Maramureș Gates
lm.note: Further east in Maramureș, you can often find more modern-style gates consisting of a black frame with corrugated metal sheets. Within this frame you can find many different patterns.

lm.name: Architecture - Moldavian Churches
lm.note: The Moldavia region (the northeast bordering Moldova) builds its churches in a distinct style. The key distinctive feature is the large semicircle ‘skirt’ roof along the back, with two smaller semicircles on the side, and a ‘witch’s hat’ roof on the spire also being quite common.

lm.name: Architecture - Mosque
lm.note: There is a Turkish minority along the Bulgarian border in Constanța county, which is the only significant muslim minority in Romania. You won’t find bilingual signs, however the Turkish presence is most apparent through the presence of mosques in Constanta and Tulcea County.

lm.name: Architecture - Neamț-Bacău Gates
lm.note: Neamț and Bacău counties have more simple versions of Suceava gates, usually missing the crossbeam underneath or the ornamentation, but still with decorated metal roofs. In Bacău especially you can find the curved variant of these roofs.

lm.name: Architecture - Oath Crosses
lm.note: In the Șușița and Gilort valleys in Gorj county, you will find these traditional oath crosses in many places. These are distinct small wooden crosses with a triangular top, often with writing on them and occurring in groups.

lm.name: Architecture - Roma Kastellos
lm.note: Wealthier Romani neighbourhoods are extremely noticeable for the over-the-top architecture, commonly featuring stacked hat roofs, sharp modern patterning, silver/gold gates and statues, and supersized versions of traditional houses even in small villages.

lm.name: Architecture - Roof Extensions
lm.note: Roofs with an extension that slopes lower than the roof itself are a moderately reliable meta for the east, but note that they can be found in the rest of the southern plain.

lm.name: Architecture - Roof Shoulders
lm.note: Roof shoulders (small tiled extensions either side of a roof end) are common in certain clusters throughout western Romania which can be helpful for a more precise regionguess.

lm.name: Architecture - Round Corners
lm.note: In Mureș county you can sometimes find houses where one of the front corners is rounded, often with some kind of crown or small tower above it.

lm.name: Architecture - Rounded Stones
lm.note: In Hunedoara you can often find these more rounded stones as a construction material for walls or house foundations.

lm.name: Architecture - Sheet Metal Fences
lm.note: These plain, thin, metal sheets in place of fences are a good indicator of the east, although they can also be found less prominently throughout the southern plain.

lm.name: Architecture - Shingle Roofs
lm.note: These shingled roofs are also a meta for the northern mountains, particularly in western Suceava. Unusually steep roofs such as the one in the image are also indicative of the same area.

lm.name: Architecture - Slab-Like Stones
lm.note: In the mountainous parts of Neamț county, stone walls and foundations are also common, but with a more slab-like appearance.

lm.name: Architecture - Small Bricks
lm.note: Houses made entirely of comparatively small bricks are common in hilly regions in western Romania.

lm.name: Architecture - Spike Finials
lm.note: In Dâmbovița, Vâlcea and Argeș counties you can commonly find simple, spike-shaped roof ornaments.

lm.name: Architecture - Stone Crosses
lm.note: In the far north-west in Satu Mare county, you can find these bold, stone crosses on people’s properties

lm.name: Architecture - Suceava Barns
lm.note: Traditional barns with asymmetrical roofs are found in the flat parts of Suceava county.

lm.name: Architecture - Suceava Colours
lm.note: In parts of Suceava county you will very often find unique shades of certain colours. The most important bright orange and dark red, commonly used in various elements of construction. Pale yellow and industrial green are less common, but also indicative of Suceava.

lm.name: Architecture - Suceava Gates
lm.note: Suceava often has traditional wooden gates similar to Maramureș, but usually with metal roofs. Suceava gates are also painted most times, as opposed to the wooden colour of Maramureș gates and have finer filigree detailing.

lm.name: Architecture - Suceava Stripes
lm.note: Suceava County has a lot of traditional houses with many unique features. One of these is vertical stripes that decorate either the gables or walls of houses. The ‘sun’ pattern on the gable in the image is also a Suceava meta.

lm.name: Architecture - Suceava Wells
lm.note: Personal wells are also very common in Suceava, usually with this very unique roof shape.

lm.name: Architecture - Székely Churches
lm.note: In Székelyland you can find all white, traditional churches (occasionally with yellow features), usually with simple spires, which are clearly non-Orthodox, as most Székely are catholic or calvinist.

lm.name: Architecture - Székely Gates
lm.note: Ornate wooden gates are also common in Székler-populated areas (see Székely), the key differences being the lack of a roof over the vehicle gate, and little pencil-top turrets on the side.

lm.name: Architecture - Transylvanian Saxon
lm.note: Transylvanian Saxon architecture is very distinct and constrained to areas which historically had many German settlers. Distinguishing features include baroque façades with plaster decor on the gable (usually including crosses and the date of construction), jerkinhead roofs, and more square versions of the twin Banat gable windows. The placement of the houses is also very distinct especially in towns, as they are mostly perpendicular to the street and connected to each other by archway-shaped driveways creating a ‘wall’ the whole length of the street.

lm.name: Architecture - Triangle Veranda
lm.note: Roofs with a triangle-shaped extension over the entrance, usually intricately decorated, can be found in much of the northeast.

lm.name: Architecture - Western Hills House
lm.note: These houses with stone foundations, small stairs and façades featuring lots of glass in a carved wooden frame are commonly found in the western hills of the southern plain, particularly in Vâlcea and Gorj county.

lm.name: Architecture - X Barns
lm.note: In the foothills of the southwest, you can often find these open hay barns with X-shaped wall patterns.

lm.name: Landscape - Apuseni Mountains
lm.note: The Apuseni mountains form a bulge of mountains geologically unrelated to the wider Carpathians. These mountains are substantially less forested than the Carpathians, and in the southern Apuseni you will find more conical mountains of volcanic origin.

lm.name: Landscape - Braşov Area
lm.note: The area just south-west of Braşov is a unique flat area with distinct mountains in all directions but north. Rather than forming chains, here you will find many isolated but very tall ridge-shaped mountains.

lm.name: Landscape - Bucegi National Park
lm.note: Bucegi National Park has a unique high-mountain landscape with almost no trees and golden grass.

lm.name: Landscape - Buzău Hills
lm.note: Around the south side of the bend in the Carpathian mountain range, you can find a unique landscape of dry, craggy hills, often with an exposed, pale underlayer.

lm.name: Landscape - Central Hills
lm.note: Relatively bare, rolling agricultural hills can be found in much of the Transylvania depression, just east of the Apuseni mountains. Further east of this zone, closer to the Carpathians, the hills will be comparatively more forested.

lm.name: Landscape - Covasna-Harghita Plains
lm.note: Flat plains surrounded by hills cover much of Covasna and southern Harghita counties. These are higher altitude than other flat regions, and therefore have more of a dead feel, with fewer trees and more potato fields rather than corn.

lm.name: Landscape - Făgăraș Plain
lm.note: The Făgăraș plain is an extremely easy to identify landscape. It is the only dead-flat part of Central Romania, and has a wall of tall mountains to its south.

lm.name: Landscape - Tulcea Hills
lm.note: Much of Tulcea is covered in low hills which combined with southeast climate and architecture can make for very unique rounds. Note that the western half of this area is covered in forested hills, whereas in the eastern half the hills are mostly treeless.

lm.name: Vegetation - Blackberry
lm.note: Blackberries (Rubus sp.) can be identified as low-lying thorny shrubs with characteristic five-part leaves. They are found in the foothills of the central and western mountains.

lm.name: Vegetation - Hoary Cress
lm.note: Hoary cress (Lepidium draba) can be identified by dense clusters of white blossoms and leaves that hug the flower stalk. They are found most often in three hot spots across the country, namely the counties of Teleorman, Constanța and Iași. Topography can be very useful to tell these three regions apart, generally speaking Teleorman is dead flat, Constanța has slight hills and wind farms will usually be visible, whereas Iași has larger hills and you can often see trees planted next to the road.

lm.name: Vegetation - Mullein
lm.note: Mulleins (Verbascum sp.) are found most often in and around Vaslui county, but beware that they can also be seen randomly throughout the country.

lm.name: Vegetation - Russian Olive
lm.note: Russian olive (Elaeagnus angustifolia) is a small tree or large bush characterized by particularly white leaves. It can be seen mainly in the east of the country. Be careful not to confuse it with the more common white willow (Salix alba), Russian olive has comparatively whiter leaves and tends to be more unruly-looking.

lm.name: Vegetation - Vineyards
lm.note: While small, individual vineyards can be found all over the place, large concentrations of vineyards are mostly unique to the foothills just west of Focşani. Large vineyards can occasionally be found in the southeast just west of Constanța.

lm.name: Romania
lm.note: Italy, Romania, Serbia, and Slovenia all look about the same. Thankfully Romania will not have a white/silver border.

lm.name: KM Marker
lm.note:
Within Europe, those red/blue/white KM markers are unique to Romania, the color representing the color the road will show up on the map.

How to use:

On the side is the road number and usually on the front are two cities, the first one is the closest largest city and the second one is the closest town.

lm.name: Romanian
lm.note:
Romanian is a Romance language similar to Italian, containing the special letters: Ă, Ș and Ț.

These letters are found in Romanian aswell as some other European languages:

  • Â, used in French, Portuguese and Turkish
  • Î, used in French, Turkish and Italian

Additionally, in Turkish you can find the letter Ş, which can be confused with the Romanian Ș.

The Romanian word for street is strada, abbreviated as str. Keep in mind that the German Straße also might be abbreviated str.

lm.name: Roadlines
lm.note:
• Middle lines are often noticeably thicker than average.
  • This is especially useful to tell Romania apart from Bulgaria, which generally has thinner road lines.

lm.name: 67C Yellow Lines
lm.note: The 67C is a mountain road with all yellow road lines.

lm.name: 7C Road
lm.note: The 7C is recognisable as going through some of the most dramatic mountains in Romania, with very green and lush vegetation. It also has distinct long and spiraling roads.

lm.name: Baia Mare House Numbers
lm.note:
In the city of Baia Mare those distinct red with white outline house numbers are common.

**Note: **They were introduced in 2024 so won't be found in earlier copyrights.

lm.name: Baia Mare Street Signs
lm.note:
In the city of Baia Mare those distinct red with white outline street signs are common. They can be in the surrounding towns as well, thought usually the red will be replaced by another color.

**Note: **They were introduced in 2024 so won't be found in earlier copyrights.

lm.name: Bilingual Signs
lm.note: Bilingual signs with Hungarian are mostly found in the central regions of Covasna, Harghita and Mureş, but also less commonly near the Hungarian border.

lm.name: Bucharest Street Sign
lm.note: Street signs in Bucharest will often have written "sector" on them which means "district" and can be found within the city. Sometimes the sign can look very similar to the Paris street sign: big, blue and with a green outline.

lm.name: Buzău Street Sign
lm.note: Street signs in Buzău will often have this logo on them resembling the letter B.

lm.name: Cluj Napoca Stickers
lm.note: The city of Cluj has those vertical white stickers of 3 numbers and a letter.

lm.name: Constanța Street Sign
lm.note: Street signs in Constanța will often be white with a black,thin border but will also have this distinct logo on them.

lm.name: Eastern Pole Sticker
lm.note: In north-east Romania the yellow stickers on the poles are usually very long. The name of the town/village can often be found in the middle of the sticker.

lm.name: Maramureș Wooden Gate
lm.note: Elaborately decorated wooden gates can be found in Maramureș, in the North-West

lm.name: Metal/Fake Tiled Roofs
lm.note: In the eastern half of Romania, it is very common to have plastic fake tiled or metal roofs. As well as the roofs seem to have more diverse colors. If most roofs you see are metal or plastic fake tiled, you are likely in the eastern half. In the center there is a combination of different roof types

lm.name: North-West Pole Stickers
lm.note:
In north-west Romania you can find those red electricity warning which are on a white background. In the rest of the country the background is mostly yellow. The North-West region can also have yellow background on the warning sign

Note: You can find similar sticks in other regions but it's by far the most common in the north-west

lm.name: Orange Tiled Roofs
lm.note: In the western half of Romania, it is very common to have orange tiled roofs. If most roofs you see are orange tiled, you are likely in the western half. In the center there is a combination of different roof types

lm.name: Orange Vertical Stickers
lm.note:
Orange vertical pole stickers with numbers on them can be found in Bucharest, Galati, Iasi, Piatra Neamt, Baia Mare and Craiova.

Note: In Iasi the sticker is 6 digits long, in the other cities it is usually 5 digits long.

lm.name: Sibiu squinting eye
lm.note: The city of Sibiu often has those windows at roof level which look like a squinting eye.

lm.name: South Stickers
lm.note:
In south-center Romania there are often stickers on poles that can give the region away.

Besides the well known rectangle stickers, within the south of Romania there are also those brown E stickers and also green D stickers.

Note: The stickers can be used interchangeably, if you see any one of those stickers then it is that region.

lm.name: Southern Pole sticker
lm.note: In south-center Romania there are often small green rectangles. If they can be read, the first 2 letters are abbreviation of the county you are in.

lm.name: Timisoara QR Stickers
lm.note: Within Timisoara a lot of the poles have those vertical stickers with 5 numbers and a QR code at the top.

lm.name: Transylvania Roof Crosses
lm.note:
In Transylvania it's not uncommon to see crosses on top of the roof, the darker areas are where there is a very high concentration of roof crosses and the lighter areas it's still common but you might have to move a bit to find them. This meta can slightly "bleed" into the neighboring counties around the border. In Maramures county a variant of the cross can be found with an arch above it!

Note: It is extremely rare to find crosses on roofs outside of those areas, so rare that I'm not sure they exist since I didn't find any.

lm.name: Using County Signs
lm.note:
Fairly often you'll see those big signs which usually are blue or white and can tell you exactly where you are.

Some useful words

  • Județ(abbreviated as jud.) - County (can be read while zooming in the dotted lines)
  • Municipiul - City
  • Localitate - City
  • Comună/Sat - Village

lm.name: Using KM Markers
lm.note: Often on the side of the road KM markers can be found in different colors (red, blue, yellow, white) and the color should also represent the color the road will show up on the map. On the side is the road number and usually on the front are two cities, the first one is the closest largest city and the second one is the closest town.

lm.name: Wind Farms
lm.note: Wind turbine farms can be found in the very east of Romania in the counties of Constanța and Tulcea, as well as in the west.

lm.name: green tag
lm.note: A small green Tag with 2 letters and a few digits. The two letters are the abbreviations of the county.

lm.name: holey pole
lm.note: Concrete holey poles with wide holes and usually painted white at the bottom are common in Romania. They are similar to poles in Poland and Hungary, but Polish poles have smaller holes that don’t go all the way to the bottom or top, and Hungarian poles typically have smaller holes as well.

lm.name: large yellow sticker
lm.note:
Large yellow sticker with the town name on it.

NOTE: Yellow sticker are common everywhere in Romania, but there are significant smaller.

lm.name: triangle top
lm.note:
These pole tops, with an upside down triangle shape, are a good clue for Romania.

NOTE: Serbia, Czechia, Slovakia and Alabania use similar pole tops.

lm.name: white sticker
lm.note:
A white sticker with a round waring symbole is common in the north-west of Romania.

NOTE: White stickers can be found everywhere in Romania, but they usually have a triangular warning symbol.

lm.name: Brașov mountain
lm.note: Brașov has a lush green mountain with 2 towers on top and has Brașov written on the right in white letters.

lm.name: Bucharest street sign
lm.note: Bucharest has 2 different street signs, the most common one is the one on the bottom, its literally the same as the paris version but language will obviously tell the difference. The other one has the same colors and uses white arrows.

lm.name: Buzău street sign
lm.note: Buzău street signs have an orange/blue B on the left, it also says the city name under it.

lm.name: Cluj-Napoca Transport
lm.note: Cluj-Napoca uses white and pink buses and white, pink and gray trams. The city name can be seen on the side of the buses.

lm.name: Constanța street sign
lm.note: Constanța street signs have this unique orange shield logo on the left and above it is the city name written.

lm.name: Timișoara taxi
lm.note: Timișoara taxis are white, which is not unique to Timișoara, but the purple sticker on the side is. It has municipiul Timișoara taxi written on the top of it.

top.html: Romania uses standard long, white European plates with a single blue strip on the left.
top.raw: Romania uses standard long, **white** European plates with a single **blue strip** on the left.

top.html:
Romanian is a Romance language similar to Italian, containing the following special letters:

  • Ă ă
  • Ș ș
  • Ț ț

These letters are also found in some other European languages:

  • Â â, used in French, Portuguese and Turkish
  • Î î, used in French, Turkish and Italian

Additionally, in Turkish you can find the letter Ş, which can be confused with the Romanian Ș.
top.raw: Romanian is a Romance language similar to Italian, containing the following special letters: - Ă ă - Ș ș - Ț ț These letters are also found in some other European languages: - Â â, used in French, Portuguese and Turkish - Î î, used in French, Turkish and Italian Additionally, in Turkish you can find the letter Ş, which can be confused with the Romanian Ș.

top.html:
The most common types of utility poles in Romania are holey poles with the holes going all the way to the bottom. The holes are typically either quite wide or quite tall.

NOTE: Poland and Hungary also both use holey poles. Polish holey poles do not have holes near the bottom and Hungarian holey poles generally have smaller holes than in Romania.
top.raw: The most common types of utility poles in Romania are **holey poles** with the holes going all the way to the bottom. The holes are typically either quite wide or quite tall. NOTE: Poland and Hungary also both use holey poles. [Polish](https://goo.gl/maps/chLemRYUZcz7DDFL6) holey poles do not have holes near the bottom and [Hungarian](https://www.google.com/maps/@47.6425626,20.0330594,3a,75y,313.1h,93.94t/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sKeSZXDk8-kk4EYn1mVYf3Q!2e0!7i16384!8i8192) holey poles generally have smaller holes than in Romania.

top.html:
Round concrete poles are also quite common.

NOTE: These are very similar to poles found in Bulgaria.
top.raw: **Round concrete poles** are also quite common. NOTE: These are very similar to poles found in Bulgaria.

top.html:
Trees and poles will often have white painted bottoms.

NOTE: This is also common in Ukraine and parts of Russia.
top.raw: Trees and poles will often have **white painted bottoms**. NOTE: This is also common in Ukraine and parts of Russia.

top.html:
This type of extremely large yellow pole sticker is specific to Romania.

Beware that smaller stickers are also common and that both Bulgaria and Hungary can have similar ones.

NOTE: The town or city name will typically be written close to the middle of these stickers. In this case Podu Iloaiei is written.
top.raw: This type of extremely **large yellow pole** sticker is specific to Romania. Beware that [smaller stickers](https://goo.gl/maps/2Dme6waEUjKguFWWA) are also common and that both [Bulgaria](https://goo.gl/maps/TnBDLBKuq3V8JjLc9) and [Hungary](https://goo.gl/maps/dvBUfMAjvm63LBC17) can have similar ones. NOTE: The town or city name will typically be written close to the middle of these stickers. In this case Podu Iloaiei is written.

top.html:
Two support bars holding up the metal bar on pole tops, resembling an upside down triangle, can sometimes be found in Romania.

NOTE: Czechia, Slovakia, Albania and Serbia also feature this pole top.
top.raw: Two support bars holding up the metal bar on pole tops, resembling an upside down triangle, can sometimes be found in Romania. NOTE: Czechia, Slovakia, Albania and Serbia also feature this pole top.

top.html: It is very common to see waystones in Romania. They are typically fairly large, with red or blue framing with the road number on the side, or made of actual stone and somewhat rugged-looking. There is also a very small variant which is all white.
top.raw: It is very common to see **waystones** in Romania. They are typically fairly large, with red or blue framing with the road number on the side, or made of actual stone and somewhat rugged-looking. There is also a very small variant which is all white.

top.html: While there are many types of roadlines in Romania, these outer lines, consisting of short dashes with narrow spaces, can be a good clue for the country.
top.raw: While there are many types of roadlines in Romania, these outer lines, consisting of **short dashes** with **narrow spaces**, can be a good clue for the country.

top.html: Middle lines are often noticeably thicker than average. This is especially useful to tell Romania apart from Bulgaria, which generally has thinner road lines.
top.raw: Middle lines are often noticeably **thicker** than average. This is especially useful to tell Romania apart from Bulgaria, which generally has [thinner road lines](https://goo.gl/maps/6nK1dEjs41bLrkPt5).

top.html: Romanian directional signs are blue, arrow shaped, and have a white border. They will very often display the road number, which can be either red or blue.
top.raw: Romanian directional signs are blue, arrow shaped, and have a white border. They will very often display the **road number**, which can be either **red or **[**blue**](https://goo.gl/maps/62EzegUJUrbSQHwQ6).

top.html:
The most common type of town entry sign in Romania is a yellow sign displaying a speed limit and a city skyline, with a white sign displaying the town name below.

NOTE: The upper sign can also either be white or completely absent.
top.raw: The most common type of town entry sign in Romania is a **yellow sign** displaying a speed limit and a city skyline, with a **white sign** displaying the town name below. NOTE: The upper sign can also either be [white](https://goo.gl/maps/nAGuvAEn4CDn1iQu5) or [completely absent](https://www.google.com/maps/@43.9295577,23.865666,3a,15y,60.5h,84.85t,358.78r/data=!3m6!1e1!3m4!1sXfkr8gj25si9PKl8IgR9Ew!2e0!7i16384!8i8192?entry=ttu).
